# 10-palus: sources

Back-test entry `10-palus.yaml`: Palus Finance, more yield on a startup's idle cash (YC Winter 2026). Written 2026-10-22 from public material only. Quotes are verbatim. **[author]** marks a choice the public material does not make, kept as small as it could be.

Sources, with the short names used below:
- **HN**: Launch HN, 2026-03-06, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=47278980 (the founders' post and 89 comments). A comment is cited as HN/NNN, meaning https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=NNN.
- **YCL**: Launch YC post, https://www.ycombinator.com/launches/PfC-palus-finance-better-yields-on-idle-cash-for-startups-and-smbs
- **YCC**: YC company page, https://www.ycombinator.com/companies/palus-finance
- **SITE**: https://palus.finance and https://www.palus.finance/treasury (read 2026-10-22)

Status today: same customer, a wider offer. The YC page says "Palus is your startup's financial advisor". The homepage now says "The world's most advanced fractional CFO firm" (SITE). The treasury product is still on /treasury.

## The eight founder-emulation items

**1. Who (actor, segment, roles).** The founder was his own customer:
- "we realized we needed the product for our own startup’s cash reserves, and other startups in the batch started telling us they wanted this too" (HN).
- The co-founder named who it is for: "this product is for startups and SMBs that don't have the time or resources to host a fractional CFO or a full-time finance team" (HN/47283812).
- A sceptic named the two people whose time it costs: "the founder, or an ops person's time" (HN/47297953).
- *Roles.* Keel's B2B shape needs one role that lives the problem and another that decides to buy. At a funded startup the person who moves the cash every month is the one who runs finance day to day (a finance or ops lead, or a fractional CFO). The person who signs where the reserve sits is the founder-CEO. The founders aim their product and copy at founders: "We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652). So `finance_lead` is the practitioner (12 people, Parts 1 and 2) and `founder` is the decision-maker (8 people, Part 3). The same company pays.
- **[author]** The split is mine. At the smallest startups the two roles are one person. That is why one practitioner (Grace Mbeki) passes the job to a fractional CFO, and why the commercial vector is read from founders.
- *Segment*: "Startups and SMBs" banking with "Brex, Mercury, etc." (HN). **[author]** I narrowed it to US venture-backed startups within two years of a raise, to match the occasion the founder describes.

**2. What (the job).** The job is to earn more on the cash without risking it and without switching banks:
- "earn higher yields with a high-yield bond portfolio" (HN).
- "a way to earn more yield on fundraise proceeds without switching banks" (YCC, as summarised from the page).
- Context job **[author]**, worded from these: "keep the money from a raise safe and earning until the company spends it".

**3. When / where (circumstance, occasion, window).**
- "The typical startup cashflow pattern is a large infusion from a raise covering 18–24 months of burn, drawn down gradually" (HN).
- "you’re giving up yield to get same-day liquidity on cash you won’t touch for six months or more" (HN).
- The repeated moment is the monthly transfer: "easy to set up rules like ("if my bank balance falls below $X then transfer $Y from treasury")" (HN/47280293).
- **[author]** The occasion "cash decision", the window {3, MONTHS}, Frequency 2 to 3 months out of 3, and Prevalence "Most" (p_60_80) are mine. They follow from "drawn down gradually" (a monthly move), and they match 05-paidly's three-month window.

**4. Which people (comparable group).**
- "Say you (like many startups) use Mercury Treasury, Rho Treasury, Brex Treasury, etc." (HN/47280293).
- "founders who've thought about idle cash management" (HN).
- **[author]** The Importance rivals come from what the thread itself raises:
  - runway: "an extra month or two of runway", HN/47282750
  - safety above the insured limit: the SVB-style worry in HN/47279304 and HN/47279349
  - getting cash back fast: "1-2 business days", HN
  - moving money without mistakes: "no manual reconciliation between accounts", HN/47283812

**5. Who pays.**
- The company pays a fee on its own balance: "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM" (HN).
- The founder decides. The pitch is to the founder's time: "It's a one-time setup that takes five minutes. We optimized our UX for founders" (HN/47290652).
- Buyer and payer:
  - **[author]** The founder's tested item is "Nobody else", which fits the five-minute pitch.
  - "The board" is the one other role on the founder's list. The thread itself puts it there: "I am not sure I would suggest my portfolio companies to risk their treasuries" (HN/47279377). SITE also says the design follows "NVCA startup treasury guidelines".
- Purchase friction:
  - "Diligence on a new provider" comes from "it definitely takes weeks to diligence your company and the offering" (HN/47401784).
  - "A tax adviser's sign-off" comes from "they should talk to their tax advisor" (HN/47282781).
  - "Board approval of the cash policy" **[author]**.

**6. Mechanism.**
- "we built Palus to connect to your existing bank account via Plaid" (HN).
- "Our bond portfolio holds short-duration floating-rate" government-backed mortgage-backed securities, "managed by Regan Capital, which runs MBSF" (HN).
- "Liquidity is typically available in 1-2 business days" (HN).
- "All assets are held with an SEC-licensed custodian" (HN).
- "two buttons and a giant number that goes up" (HN).
- Compatibility conditions, Adoption friction efforts and the Commitment step:
  - The tested condition, "They could wait two days for their cash", is the founder's own claim: "most startups can afford to take on a bit more liquidity risk on their long-term cash (on the order of a couple of days)" (HN/47282907).
  - The commitment step comes from "I'd encourage you to start small, try us out, and grow your position over time" (HN/47280532).
  - The tested effort, "Move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury", **[author]**, worded from "The problem is the treasury product bundled with them, not the bank" (HN).

**7. Price.**
- "We will charge a flat 0.25% annual fee on AUM, compared to the 0.15–0.60%, depending on balance, charged by other treasury providers" (HN).
- "Rho charges a variable rate that peaks at 0.6% for any deposit of $2M or less" (HN/47280707).
- Yields: "we target 4.5–5% returns vs. roughly 3.5% from most money market funds" (HN). SITE now says "targeted SOFR + 1% spread".
- **[author]** Keel's price is a money range over a period, and its ladder stops below $10,000. So I state the fee per month on the reserve the founder's own example uses, $4M to $6M: 0.25% of that is $10,000 to $15,000 a year, so $800 to $1,200 a month.
- **[author]** The cost estimate, $4,000 to $6,000 a month, is the yield given up. The founder says "on $5M, it's an extra $50k-75k per year" (HN/47280107), which is about $4,200 to $6,250 a month, rounded to the range. It counts yield given up, which the registry's meaning allows ("foregone alternatives"). It does not count the 0.15% to 0.60% fee the bank's product already takes.
- **[author]** The hourly rate, $75, is mine: a startup finance lead's salary of about $150k a year, over a working year.
- Ability to pay is derived by code: 13% to 30%, small_share.

**8. Occasions (real accounts).**
- No named customer quote is public. HN is the record: batchmates "started telling us they wanted this too" (HN), one sign-up, "I’ve wanted this produce for years. Signed up." (HN/47283895), and many sceptics. Each respondent below is traced to one of them.

Decision-makers (`link: COMMERCIAL_B2B`, `founder`, Part 3 only, no story on screen):

She stands for the founders' own case ("putting $5M into Palus yields them an extra $50k-75k per year", HN/47290584) and the batchmates who "wanted this too" (HN). Her $2,000 a month is the bank's treasury fee.
- Jamal Booker: HN/47297953 ("That 50-75k is more like $5k/month out of what is typically a ~200-400k monthly burn") and HN/47401784 ("it definitely takes weeks to diligence").

- Maya Feldman: HN/47283895 (signed up) and HN/47283356 (liked "a number that goes up").

No respondent carries a commenter's handle or a real customer's name (SITE names client companies; none is used).

## Open

- **Relative advantage code.** The registry fixes five advantage codes (fewer_attempts, shorter_time, less_worry, less_help_needed, easier_recovery). None means "more money". I used `less_help_needed` with the founder's label "Higher yield without hiring for treasury". It is the closest code, and it carries the founder's claim of "no need to hire for treasury operations" (HN/47283812). A yield code would fit better.
- **Price period.** Palus prices a share of the balance, not an amount per period. The $800 to $1,200 a month depends on the $4M to $6M reserve I chose. Keel has no "percent of balance" price.
- **Cost estimate kind.** The founder's cost is yield given up, not money spent. Decision-makers asked "what it cost the team last month" will report fees and hours, so Existing sacrifice is likely to read far below the founder's estimate. That is a real finding about this idea, but it is also partly an artefact of the question's wording.
- **Window.** The {3, MONTHS} window and the "cash decision" occasion are mine. Public material has no single trigger moment, only "drawn down gradually".
- **Not checked against the engine.** The file passes keel-e2e-eval's `instructions/corpus.py` loader (bound to the registry) and every rule of `sim/check_corpus_r12.py` but S/C/V. Those three need the `expected` block, which a back-test omits by design.

insights.line: What would have made a difference?

whys.g1: Nothing is misplaced and there are no duplicate groups, but a finance lead would put all three answers in one group, 'ease and safety matter more than extra yield', and leaving each on its own hides that they agree.
whys.g2: There is no junk answer on this line; all three answers are on-topic about what would have made a difference.

screens.why1: Right after saying how Palus fits beside the bank, the obvious next question is what it does better than leaving the reserve in Mercury or Brex Treasury.

screens.why4: The only option is the box plus an *I'm not sure* chip, which is the right escape for a founder who cannot name a benefit, and my two rows went in cleanly.
screens.why5: Both rows are my own words from the launch, kept as typed with nothing added.
screens.why7: Two short rows, each under nine words and each a noun phrase naming one change against today's bank treasury, with the yield I lead with first and no number I did not write; flagging the no-hire row, which a bank treasury also delivers, is the next screen's job.

screens.why1: Right after I typed what Palus does better, Keel shows my benefits back as rows to check, which is the obvious next step before the stranger's item.
screens.why2: 'Higher yield', 'cash not needed for months' and 'treasury hire' are how a startup finance lead or founder talks, so I read it in one pass, though the joined belief sentence is clunky.
screens.why3: Both rows describe what my own startup and my batchmates live: a raise sitting idle at Mercury or Brex earning the bank-treasury rate, and nobody on staff to manage it.
screens.why4: Two rows, one gain each, distinct, in my words, matching the split I agreed to (yield on long-term cash, and no treasury hire), with the 1-to-4 guidance under them.
screens.why5: The rows are exactly my two revised benefits in my order, with nothing added and no number I did not write.
screens.why7: The rows meet the shape (two non-overlapping benefits, the lead kept, both carried in order in the belief, on the 'last time they put off managing the idle cash' hard case), but 'No treasury hire to manage it' is something the bank's own treasury product (Mercury/Brex Treasury) already gives today, and the card requires such a row to be flagged for me to keep or drop, which this screen does not do.
screens.instead: Rows: 'Higher yield on cash not needed for months' · 'More yield than the bank's treasury, same upkeep' -- with a flag on the second if it stays as 'No treasury hire': 'Your bank's treasury already needs no hire -- keep or drop?'

screens.why5: My two steps sit there word for word, with nothing added or reworded.
screens.why7: The box asks for 1 to 4 efforts of up to 9 words each, and my rows fit: both are base-form steps the finance lead takes themselves, neither is another role's sign-off or the Compatibility condition (now 'keep their current bank'), and the 'I'm not sure' escape is there as the card requires.

screens.why1: After I said what they'd have to do to start, checking the efforts Keel drafted from my words is the obvious next screen.

screens.why1: Right after I checked the efforts Keel wrote, it is obvious I now pick the one most likely to stop a finance lead, and it asks nothing already answered.
screens.why2: Plaid, the long-term reserve and the bank's treasury are the words a startup finance lead running Mercury or Brex cash uses every month, and the intro says plainly that one is picked and nothing is reworded.

screens.why5: Both rows are the efforts I gave, word for word, and the test box carries my pick unchanged: Most would move the long-term reserve out of the bank's treasury.

screens.why1: Right before the study goes out, deciding whether to collect emails from finance leads who'd try it is an obvious last step, and as a founder who got batchmates saying 'we want this too' I'd want those leads.

screens.why3: Whether I want sign-ups from strangers is my own call and I know it at once.

screens.why5: Nothing of my product is reworded here, and the line respondents see ('Would you try this for real?') leaks no product name or role.

screens.why1: Choosing who will put my questions to finance leads belongs at the last step before the link goes out, after the pilot offer, and nothing earlier asked it.

screens.why4: AI video, read-and-tap, and let them choose cover the real choices, are distinct, and each is described plainly.

screens.why_b1: 'Did not hold' sits directly beside '3 of 7 would do it · bar 5 of 7 · 2 short', so I see both the verdict and the number that decides it.

screens.why_b6: The quotes add things I did not type: blame is asymmetric ('nobody asks why we earned a bit less, they'd ask why we lost any'), monthly bill-paying makes two-click liquidity beat a point of yield, Marcus wants a better rate inside the bank he already uses, and the accountant wants plain cash for the tax break.

screens.why1: As the opening screener, it obviously checks whether I'm one of the startup finance people this study is for before asking anything else.
screens.why2: I'd answer on first read, but Mercury and Brex are fintechs on top of partner banks rather than banks, and 'a similar bank' is fuzzy: does a startup that also keeps money at JPMorgan or a treasury account count?
screens.why3: I run our accounts, so I know exactly where our cash sits.
screens.why4: A gate takes a plain yes or no with no escape, and that's what it has.
screens.why5: Mercury and Brex are just how I'd describe our banking, and nothing of a product or plan comes through.
screens.why6: It's short, one question, and easy to answer by ear, though 'Yes or no' would say more naturally than 'I'll read 2 options.'
screens.instead: Does your startup keep its operating cash with Mercury, Brex or a similar startup-focused bank? Yes or no.

screens.why1: Right after confirming we bank with Mercury or Brex, asking whether something went wrong with the raise money in the window is the obvious next step for a gate.
screens.why2: I'd follow it on first hearing, but nobody in my seat says 'raise cash'; I'd say 'the cash from our raise' or 'our treasury', and 'yield dropped' is ambiguous between the market rate falling and our own money earning less.
screens.why3: I know what our sweep or treasury account pays and whether it went down; I watch it, roughly 3.2% when we last checked.
screens.why4: Yes and No are complete and distinct for a gate; the 'cash balance' chips read oddly but belong to the story box, not the gate.
screens.why5: A yield drop is a market move that happens to me, not the founder's likely problem of our money sitting idle or earning less than it could, so the meaning has drifted a little, though nothing of the product leaks.
screens.why6: Short, one question, 'Yes or no' said cleanly; easy to answer on one hearing.
screens.why7: Yes and No are both on the gate's fixed pair with no escape, but a rate-driven yield drop hits nearly everyone holding cash in a sweep or treasury product, so the event leans toward the shared circumstance and No would have few true takers.
screens.instead: In the last 3 months, did cash from your raise sit in an account earning little or nothing? Yes · No

screens.why1: After two screens on where our raise cash sits and whether its yield dropped, showing the idea at the start of part 2 is the obvious next step.
screens.why2: Treasury account, money market fund, custodian and Plaid are my everyday words, but I'd say runway or excess cash, not 'long-term reserve', and the four-adjective stack before 'mortgage bonds' takes a second read.
screens.why3: Where our raise cash sits, how fast it comes back to checking and what it yields against a money market fund is exactly what I deal with.
screens.why4: A card to read, with no options.
screens.why5: It's shown on purpose as an idea, the claim is put on 'the people building it', and no internal roles or jargon reach me beyond the product itself.
screens.why6: Heard once, 'a managed portfolio of short-duration, floating-rate, government-backed mortgage bonds' is a mouthful, and the second line opening 'A treasury account links...' sounds like a restart rather than 'It links...'.
screens.instead: Imagine Palus, a treasury account that holds your spare cash in government-backed mortgage bonds. It links to your bank through Plaid, keeps the bonds short-term and floating-rate, holds them in your company's name at a regulated custodian, and returns cash to checking in one to two business days. The people building it believe it would earn 4.5 to 5 percent, against about 3.5 percent from a money market fund after its fee.

screens.why1: Right after the Palus card, asking whether I could live with a one-to-two-day wait to get money out is the obvious first thing to check about parking our reserve in bonds instead of Mercury.
screens.why2: 'Your last cash balance' isn't a moment I can picture, and 'waited for your cash' doesn't say waited for what; I'd read it twice to land on 'pulling money out of the reserve'.
screens.why3: I know our payroll and spend timing cold, so I can say whether a T+1/T+2 delay would hurt, but without a real occasion like the last time I moved money out I'm half guessing which moment counts.
screens.why4: The four plus I can't tell are distinct and cover it, but 'Yes, most of the time' and 'Only sometimes' sit oddly on one single occasion.
screens.why5: The one-to-two-business-day condition is kept as written, and nothing beyond the deliberately shown idea card leaks.
screens.why6: Two short sentences and four short options, said as a list I can hold, with one escape at the end.
screens.why7: It has the ability four in order with the escape apart, and it can go either way across startups so it can hold or fail; but the anchor isn't a real occasion, so the 'could you have, on that occasion' measure is loose.
screens.instead: Think of the last time you moved money out of your reserve to cover spending. Could you have waited one to two business days for it to arrive? Yes, easily · Yes, most of the time · Only sometimes · No · I can't tell

screens.why1: Right after the reveal and the wait-for-cash question, asking whether Palus would have beaten how we placed our raise cash is the obvious next thing to ask.
screens.why2: Treasury account and reserve are my words, but 'decided where cash from a raise sits until it is needed' is stiff, and 'done that better' leaves me unsure whether it means a better yield or a better decision, since Palus doesn't make the decision.
screens.why3: I made that call after our raise, keeping it at Mercury in a sweep at about 3.2%, so I can answer from what I actually did.
screens.why4: The four answers cover it, from a lot better to worse, and I can't tell fits as the escape; I'd honestly say no difference because the operational burden matters more to me than yield.
screens.why5: The question names Palus the same way the card just did, and nothing beyond the shown idea leaks into it.
screens.why6: The stem runs past 30 words with a long occasion clause before the question, which is a lot to hold on one hearing, though the options read as a clean short list.
screens.why7: The measure, the four fixed answers, the balance and the escape are all right, but the occasion is the routine circumstance rather than the hard case the study already asked about (the yield on raise cash dropping), so the hurt rule is bent.
screens.instead: Think of the most recent time the yield on your raise cash dropped. Would Palus, a treasury account for your long-term reserve, have handled that better for you, or not? A lot better · A little better · No difference · Worse · I can't tell

screens.why1: After the idea card and the earlier questions, asking whether I would actually move the reserve to use it is the obvious last question.

screens.why5: Only the idea card on purpose reaches me, and moving the reserve out of the bank's treasury is a plain step in my words, not founder jargon.
screens.why6: Heard once it is one short question with four short options and one escape, easy to hold.
